## Data Repositories

:::{.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="false"}
### {{< fa brain >}} Learning Objectives

After completing this topic you will be able to: 

- <u>Understand</u> the differences between generalist repositories, more specialized repositories, and search aggregators.
- <u>Identify</u> some repositories "known for" particular types of data

:::

When you start a synthesis research project, you may already have some datasets in-hand at the outset but it is likely that **you will need to find more data to test your hypotheses**. Research data repositories are organizations or facilities that are primarily dedicated to storing and managing research data, so they are a great place to find and access relevant data for answering your research question. There are _a lot_ of data repositories out there. In fact, the Registry of Research Data Repositories ([re3data.org](https://www.re3data.org/)) lists 3526 repositories at the time of writing, so you probably can't search them all exhaustively. It helps to know the landscape and search efficiently.

::: {.callout-tip}

## A word about metadata and searching repositories

:::{style="float: right; width: 40%;  margin: 0.5em 0 1em 1.5em; text-align: left;"}

![A **dataset** is one or more data files AND the metadata describing those data. It is a good idea to keep data and metadata together forever.](topics/images/figure_a-dataset.png){fig-alt="A figure showing a folder with data and metadata files inside"}

:::

We're about describe a bunch of repositories, and then move on to strategies for searching them. It is first worth mentioning that, while we visit repositories to access the many, many data files they contain, every repository (so far as we know) also publishes **metadata** describing those data. If you've never heard of metadata before, the quick definition is "data about the data," or information describing a unit of data. Metadata usually contains information about:

- **who** collected the data
- **what** was collected
- **when**, **where**, **how** and **why** the data were collected.

When you search in a repository or aggregator, _you are not searching the data themselves, you are searching the metadata._ The metadata contain essential information that you need to understand the data, evaluate if they are fit for your research purpose, and use in your analysis. So, research data should always be accompanied by descriptive metadata, a combination we refer to as a **dataset**. Keep the dataset concept, and the value of metadata, in mind as you search for data, and as you create your own synthesis data products.

:::

We can categorize repositories a few different ways, though keep in mind that these categories are more of a spectrum. **Generalist repositories** hold all kinds of data from all sorts of research. They tend to have fairly lax requirements for metadata and data quality, so you may have to sift through your search results carefully to determine if a dataset is fit for use. **Domain-specific repositories** specialize in data from a particular domain, such as a scientific discipline (e.g. environmental science or biomedical research), region (e.g. Arctic data), or research community (e.g. USGS). They tend to have higher metadata standards for the data they accept into the repository. **Data specialist** repositories specialize in publishing a limited number of data types. They may only accept data from specific sources or research networks (e.g. NEON) and usually have strict requirements for metadata and data formatting. These differences in repository specialization can have big impacts on how much time you spend finding useful data and getting it ready to analyze.

![There is a gradient in repository specialization (domain, metadata/data standards) and how Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) the data are. Adapted from Gries et al. 2023](topics/images/figure_data-repos-conceptual.png){width=70% fig-align="center" fig-alt="A figure showing the research data repositories as circles along a spectrum of specialization and FAIR-ness"}

At most repositories you can search and access data through a graphical interface on the website, or by writing calls to an underlying "application programming interface", or **API**. You may need to read the repository's documentation to understand and use the API directly, but often repositories provide "wrappers" for the API written in your favorite programming language that make it easier. Something you'll notice as you interact with repositories in 2026 is that many require you to create an account and login to access data. Although it may seem antithethetical to open science policies, authentication requirements are becoming the norm as repositories protect their systems and data from malicious actors and "bot" traffic (often AI-driven) on the internet. For now, be prepared to make an account to access data, and later in the course we will provide some guidance on low-friction ways to securely[^1] authenticate with your repository credentials when you use scripts and API calls.

Below we present three non-exhaustive lists of ecology and environmental data repositories that have proven useful to other synthesis projects in the past. They are broken into categories as above, and listed in alphabetical order. The "{{< fa brands r-project >}} Package" column links to packages that can be used to find and access data from the repository in an R script (these are API wrappers, essentially). If it contains the GitHub logo ({{< fa brands github >}}) then the package is available on GitHub but not on CRAN (or not available at time of writing). The "In DataONE" column indicates whether the repository's holdings are indexed in [DataONE](https://search.dataone.org), which is a search aggregator, as explained below.

[^1]: One quick reminder here is that if you are accessing APIs with a script, **never paste your private credentials into something you will push to GitHub!** We'll return to this later.

:::{.panel-tabset}

### Domain-specific repositories

| **Name** | **Description** | {{< fa brands r-project >}} **Package** | **In DataONE** | 
|:---:|:---|:---:|:---:|
| [Arctic Data Center](https://arcticdata.io/) | The primary NSF-funded repository for Arctic research data, accepting observational, experimental, and modeling data from multiple disciplines. Uses EML metadata and operates as a DataONE member node. | [`dataone`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dataone/index.html) | {{< fa check >}} |
| [BCO-DMO](https://www.bco-dmo.org/) | The Biological and Chemical Oceanography Data Management Office serves NSF-funded ocean science projects, curating biological, chemical, and physical oceanographic data from research cruises, moorings, and laboratory experiments. Marine and coastal LTER sites often publish data here. | -- | {{< fa check >}} |
| [EDI](https://edirepository.org/) | Contains a wide range of ecological and environmental datasets, including long-term observational data, experimental results, and field studies from diverse ecosystems. Specializes in detailed metadata (as EML) and is one of the primary repositories for LTER data. | [`EDIutils`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/EDIutils/index.html) | {{< fa check >}} |
| [ESS-DIVE](https://ess-dive.lbl.gov/) | The Environmental System Science Data Infrastructure for a Virtual Ecosystem (ESS-DIVE) includes a variety of observational, experimental, modeling and other data products from a wide range of ecological and urban systems. Used by many Department of Energy funded science programs. | -- | {{< fa check >}} |
| [NASA](https://data.nasa.gov/) | Provides data on earth science, space exploration, and climate, including satellite imagery and observational data for both terrestrial and extraterrestrial studies. Nice GUI-based data download via [AppEEARS](https://appeears.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov/). | [`nasadata`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nasadata/index.html) | -- |
| [ORNL DAAC](https://daac.ornl.gov/) | One of NASA's Distributed Active Archive Centers (DAACs), based at Oak Ridge National Lab. Specializing in terrestrial ecology and biogeochemical dynamics and including field campaign, remote sensing, and model archive data with detailed user guides for each product. | -- | -- |
| [PANGAEA](https://pangaea.de/) | A curated repository based in Europe for a wide range of Earth and environmental science data. Frequently used to deposit data as supplements to journal articles. | [`pangaear`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pangaear/index.html) | {{< fa check >}} |
| [USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/products/data/all-data) | Hosts data on geology, hydrology, biology, and geography, including topographical maps and natural resource assessments. | [`dataRetrieval`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dataRetrieval/index.html) | {{< fa check >}} |

: Domain-specific repositories accepting a broad range of data. These publish multiple data types and generally maintain higher metadata standards than generalist repositories, though the data may not be well-standardized. {#tbl-domain-repos}

| [OpenTopography](https://opentopography.org/) | Provides high-resolution topographic data, including lidar point clouds, derived rasters, and global elevation products, with on-demand processing tools for generating DEMs and derivative products. | -- | {{< fa check >}} |

: Highly specialized repositories that require standardized sampling, data formats, and/or metadata. Many of these repositories are also specific to a particular research domain or network. {#tbl-specialized-repos}


### Generalist repositories

| **Name** | **Description** | {{< fa brands r-project >}} **Package** | **In DataONE** | 
|:---:|:---|:---:|:---:|
| [Dryad](https://datadryad.org/) | A curated, nonprofit repository for data underlying scientific publications, with a focus on biosciences. Accepts any file format, applies CC0 to all submissions, and assigns DOIs. Widely used to satisfy journal data-availability requirements. | [`rdryad`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rdryad/index.html)* | {{< fa check >}} |
| [Figshare](https://figshare.com/) | A general-purpose repository for figures, datasets, posters, preprints, and other research outputs. Minimal metadata requirements, DOIs on deposit, and a generous file-size allowance make it a quick option for supplementary materials. | {{< fa brands github >}} [`deposits`](https://github.com/ropenscilabs/deposits) | -- |
| [Harvard Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/) | An open repository hosting datasets across all disciplines, organized into individual "dataverses" that let projects or institutions manage their own collections. Supports versioning, DOIs, and a structured citation metadata block. | [`dataverse`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dataverse/index.html) | {{< fa check >}} |
| [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) | A general-purpose repository operated by CERN, accepting any file type or discipline. Integrates directly with GitHub to archive software releases and mint DOIs, with a concept DOI that always resolves to the latest version. | [`zen4R`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/zen4R/index.html) | -- |

: Generalist repositories accepting a broad range of data types with minimal metadata requirements. Be aware that it can be difficult to separate the "wheat from the chaff." R packages marked with an asterisk (*) are being deprecated soon.

:::

### Searching _across_ repositories

If you don't find everything you're looking for in a particular data repository, you might want to consider a broader search across many repositories. There are a few data search aggregators out there that are quite useful for this. These services collect or index metadata from many repositories and allow you to search them in one interface. They do not always provide the data directly, instead linking out to the source repository. **Be careful to screen out duplicate results if you search directly in repositories and then in aggregators where those repositories are listed.**

| **Name** | **Description** | {{< fa brands r-project >}} **Package** |
|:---:|:---|:---:|
| [DataONE](https://www.dataone.org/) | Aggregates environmental and ecological data from global sources, focusing on biodiversity, climate, and ecosystem research. | [`dataone`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dataone/index.html) |
| [Google Dataset Search](https://datasetsearch.research.google.com/) | Google Dataset Search crawls schema.org metadata published on repository landing pages to make datasets discoverable across thousands of sources at once. Useful as a starting point when the holding repository is unknown, but coverage depends on how well each repository exposes its metadata. | -- |
| [OpenAIRE EXPLORE](https://explore.openaire.eu) | OpenAIRE is a central organization in the European Commission's open science initiative. The EXLORE tool indexes dataset metadata from thousands of repositories, journals, registries and other sources. Data sources are worldwide, not just European. | {{< fa brands github >}} [OpenAIRE](https://github.com/KTH-Library/OpenAIRE/) |
| [Open Traits Network](https://opentraits.org/datasets.html) | The Open Traits Network has compiled an extensive lists of repositories for trait data. Check out their repository inventory for trait data. | -- |

### More resources

- The executive branch agencies of the U.S. federal government collect lots of data. They are distributed across many repositories, which makes it a little difficult to know where to look. The [Federal Data Field Guide](https://www.federaldatafieldguide.us) explains the federal data landscape, and the [Data.gov catalog](https://catalog.data.gov/) provides a fairly comprehensive listing of published federal datasets.
